content: Defecation is the physiological process by which organisms expel solid or semisolid waste material, known as feces, from the digestive tract through the anus. In humans, the frequency of defecation varies widely, ranging from several times a day to a few times per week. For example, sloths can go up to a week without defecating. The movement of fecal matter through the digestive tract is facilitated by waves of muscular contractions called peristalsis, which propel the material toward the rectum. Undigested food may also be expelled during this process, which is referred to as egestion. The rectum, specifically the rectal ampulla (also known as the ampulla recti), serves as a temporary storage site for waste material. As the rectum fills with fecal matter, its walls expand, activating stretch receptors in the rectal walls. These receptors send signals to the nervous system, creating the sensation or urge to defecate. If this urge is ignored, the material in the rectum may be returned to the colon, where additional water is absorbed. Prolonged delays in defecation can lead to the hardening of fecal matter, resulting in constipation. During this process, the rectum shortens as fecal material is pushed into the anal canal by peristaltic waves. The internal and external anal sphincters play a critical role in controlling the passage of feces. These sphincters must relax to allow the expulsion of waste, while muscles surrounding the anus contract to assist in the process by pulling the anus upward over the exiting feces. Defecation involves the coordinated effort of several muscle groups, including the chest muscles, diaphragm, abdominal wall muscles, and pelvic diaphragm. The physiological stress experienced during defecation is similar to that of the Valsalva maneuver. The act of defecation requires conscious relaxation of the external anal sphincter muscles. Interestingly, the anal and urethral sphincter muscles are closely linked. Research conducted by Dr. Harrison Weed at the Ohio State University Medical Center has demonstrated that these muscles cannot contract independently of one another and that both relax simultaneously during urination. This physiological connection explains why defecation is often accompanied by urination. Defecation can be either voluntary or involuntary. Young children acquire voluntary control over this process through toilet training. Once this control is established, involuntary defecation, or fecal incontinence, may occur due to various factors, including physical trauma (e.g., damage to the anal sphincter during an episiotomy), severe fright, inflammatory bowel disease, impaired water absorption in the colon (as seen in diarrhea), or psychological and neurological conditions. Cultural practices influence the positions and methods used for defecation. In many parts of South Asia, East Asia, and rural areas of the Middle East, squatting is the customary position, often facilitated by squat toilets. In contrast, most Western countries use sit-down toilets. After defecation, the anus and surrounding area may be cleaned using toilet paper or similar products. In some cultures, water is also used for cleansing, as with bidets. In Japan, advanced toilets known as washlets are designed to wash and dry the anus automatically after defecation.
